```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5,
       col = if (identical(highlight, "DATA")) "lightskyblue1" else NA)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}
```

No packages beyond base R are needed.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
sections 4.1 (why variability matters, pp. 140-141), 4.2 (basic
probability theory, pp. 141-145), and 4.3 (Bayes' rule, pp. 145-152).

# Adding and multiplying probabilities {#lab3}

Two rules do most of the work of combining probabilities: add the
probabilities of outcomes that can't happen together, and multiply the
probabilities of independent events. This part sets up those rules,
plus the language of sample spaces and events. Everything else on the
page is built from them.

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-models, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("MODELS")
```

Ecological data vary for several reasons (Bolker 4.1). Measurements
are imprecise. Individuals with the same expected fate live or die by
chance (demographic stochasticity). Rates themselves change from place
to place and year to year (environmental stochasticity). A
data-generating model (MODELS) describes that variation with
probability, so the rules of probability are the grammar for writing
models down and, later, for fitting them.

## 2. Sample spaces and events {#sample-space}

A pine seed that lands on the forest floor ends up with exactly one of
four fates: eaten by a rodent, eaten by a bird, germinating, or dying in
the soil. Those four outcomes make up the **sample space**, the set of
everything that could happen. An **event** is any set of outcomes:
"eaten" is the event {rodent, bird}. A **probability** assigns each
event a number, following three rules (Kolmogorov's axioms):

1. No probability is negative: $P(A) \ge 0$.
2. Something in the sample space happens: $P(\text{all outcomes}) = 1$.
3. If $A$ and $B$ can't happen together (they are **mutually
   exclusive**), $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

```{r seed-fates}
fates <- c(rodent = 0.35, bird = 0.15, germinate = 0.10, soil = 0.40)
sum(fates)                              # rule 2
fates["rodent"] + fates["bird"]         # P(eaten), by rule 3
1 - fates["germinate"]                  # P(does not germinate)
```

A seed can't be eaten by a rodent and by a bird, so
$P(\text{eaten}) = 0.35 + 0.15 = 0.50$. The last line uses a
consequence of rules 2 and 3, the **complement rule**:
$P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$, since $A$ and "not $A$" are mutually
exclusive and together cover everything.

## 3. Multiplying probabilities {#multiplication}

**A probability times a count gives an expected count.** If 200 seeds
fall and each is eaten by a rodent with probability 0.35, expect
$200 \times 0.35 = 70$ rodent-eaten seeds. The actual number will vary
around 70 from one batch of seeds to the next.

**Independent events multiply.** Two observers search the same plot
for nests without talking to each other. Each finds a given nest with
probability 0.6. If finding a nest is independent between observers,
the chance that both find it is $0.6 \times 0.6$. The four possible
outcomes for one nest:

```{r double-observer}
p_find <- 0.6
outcomes <- c(both     = p_find * p_find,
              only_1   = p_find * (1 - p_find),
              only_2   = (1 - p_find) * p_find,
              neither  = (1 - p_find) * (1 - p_find))
outcomes
sum(outcomes)
1 - outcomes["neither"]                 # P(at least one observer finds it)
```

The four outcomes are mutually exclusive and add to 1. "At least one
observer finds it" has probability `r f2(1 - (1 - p_find)^2)`, which
is easiest to get from the complement (neither finds it, 0.16).

Adding the two observers' probabilities, $0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2$, can't be
right. The two events overlap (both observers can find the same nest),
so the overlap gets counted twice. The general addition rule subtracts
it once:

$$P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.6 + 0.6 - 0.36 = 0.84.$$

> **Question:** Real nests differ in how well they are hidden, so a
> nest one observer misses is often missed by the other too. Is the
> true chance that both miss a nest more or less than 0.16? What does
> that do to an estimate of how many nests nobody found?

# Conditional probability and Bayes' rule {#bayes-rule}

Conditional probability describes how knowing one thing changes the
probability of another. Rearranged, it gives Bayes' rule, which turns
the probability of the data under a hypothesis into the probability of
the hypothesis given the data. The WOD for this class (WODs are short
warm-up exercises that open each lecture) was a puzzle about dice,
lottery tickets, and shared birthdays; it is worked through with the
[counting material](Week4_ProbabilityDistributions.html#wod-puzzle).

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-fit, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("FIT")
```

A model tells us how likely the data are if a hypothesis is true,
$P(\text{data} \mid \text{hypothesis})$. What we usually want is the
reverse: how believable is each hypothesis, given the data? The two
are different numbers, and Bayes' rule converts one into the other.
The probability of the data under a hypothesis is called the
**likelihood**, and it drives the FIT step for the rest of the course.

## 2. Joint, marginal, and conditional probability {#conditional}

A survey of a woodland plot records 241 trees by species and by
whether they carry mistletoe:

```{r tree-table}
trees <- matrix(c(39, 76, 101, 25), nrow = 2,
                dimnames = list(status = c("infested", "healthy"),
                                species = c("juniper", "pinyon")))
trees
p_trees <- trees / sum(trees)           # joint probabilities
round(p_trees, 3)
```

Pick one tree at random. The **joint probability** that it is both a
healthy tree and a pinyon is one cell divided by the total,
$P(\text{healthy and pinyon}) = 25/241 =$ `r f3(25/241)`. A
**marginal probability** ignores one attribute by summing over it:

```{r tree-marginal}
p_status  <- rowSums(trees) / sum(trees)
p_species <- colSums(trees) / sum(trees)
p_status
p_species
```

**Multiplying marginals doesn't give the joint probability here:**

```{r tree-product}
p_status["healthy"] * p_species["pinyon"]   # product of marginals
p_trees["healthy", "pinyon"]                # actual joint probability
```

The product, `r f3(p_status["healthy"] * p_species["pinyon"])`, is
about twice the true value, `r f3(p_trees["healthy", "pinyon"])`.
Multiplying only works for independent events, and these two aren't:
pinyons here are mostly infested.

**Conditional probability** narrows the sample space. Among pinyons
only, what fraction are healthy?

$$P(\text{healthy} \mid \text{pinyon}) =
\frac{P(\text{healthy and pinyon})}{P(\text{pinyon})}.$$

```{r tree-conditional}
p_trees["healthy", "pinyon"] / p_species["pinyon"]    # = 25 / 126
p_trees["healthy", "juniper"] / p_species["juniper"]  # = 76 / 115
```

Dividing by $P(\text{pinyon})$ throws out the junipers and rescales
what's left so it adds to 1. A pinyon is healthy with probability
`r f3(25/126)`; a juniper, `r f3(76/115)`.

Rearranging the definition gives the **multiplication rule**, which
holds whether or not the events are independent:

$$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B)\, P(B).$$

Two events are **independent** when $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$: knowing $B$
doesn't change the probability of $A$. Only then does the rule
simplify to $P(A)\,P(B)$. Nearly every likelihood in this course
multiplies probabilities of separate observations, so it quietly
assumes independence.

**Law of total probability.** A tree is either a pinyon or a juniper,
so the chance it is healthy is a weighted average of the two
conditional probabilities:

$$P(\text{healthy}) = P(\text{healthy} \mid \text{pinyon})\,P(\text{pinyon})
+ P(\text{healthy} \mid \text{juniper})\,P(\text{juniper}).$$

```{r total-probability}
(25 / 126) * p_species["pinyon"] + (76 / 115) * p_species["juniper"]
```

This matches the marginal, `r f3(p_status["healthy"])`. (Bolker writes
this rule on p. 142 as $P(A) = P(A \mid B) + P(A \mid \text{not } B)$,
leaving out the weights; the weights are needed.)

In the widget, the square has area 1. The column widths are $P(A)$ and
$P(\text{not } A)$, and the blue height in each column is the
conditional probability of $B$ in that column, so every area is a joint
probability. The "Tree plot" button sets $A$ = pinyon and $B$ =
healthy.

```{r area-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("prob_area.html")
```

> **Question:** Start from the tree plot settings and move
> $P(B \mid \text{not } A)$ until the top of the blue region is level
> across both columns. What happens to $P(A \mid B)$, and how does it
> compare with $P(A)$? What does a level line say about whether species
> tells you anything about infestation?

## 3. Bayes' rule {#bayes}

The multiplication rule works in either order:

$$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A).$$

Divide by $P(B)$:

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}.$$

That's **Bayes' rule**, a recipe for turning a conditional probability
around. For the trees, the chance that a healthy tree is a pinyon:

```{r bayes-trees}
p_healthy_given_pinyon <- 25 / 126
p_healthy_given_pinyon * p_species["pinyon"] / p_status["healthy"]
25 / 101                                    # straight from the table
```

$P(\text{healthy} \mid \text{pinyon}) =$ `r f3(25/126)` and
$P(\text{pinyon} \mid \text{healthy}) =$ `r f3(25/101)`. They answer
different questions, and confusing them is the most common error with
conditional probability.

**False positives in medical testing** (Bolker 4.3.1). A disease
infects one person in a million, $P(I) = 10^{-6}$. A test never misses
an infection, $P(+ \mid I) = 1$, but gives a false positive to 1% of
uninfected people, $P(+ \mid U) = 0.01$. If you test positive, how
likely are you to be infected?

Bayes' rule needs $P(+)$, the overall chance of a positive test. A
positive comes from either an infected or an uninfected person, so the
law of total probability gives

$$P(+) = P(+ \mid I)\,P(I) + P(+ \mid U)\,P(U).$$

```{r medical-test}
p_inf <- 1e-6
p_pos_inf <- 1
p_pos_unf <- 0.01

p_pos <- p_pos_inf * p_inf + p_pos_unf * (1 - p_inf)
p_pos
p_inf_pos <- p_pos_inf * p_inf / p_pos
p_inf_pos
```

A positive test means a `r format(signif(p_inf_pos, 2), scientific = FALSE)`
chance of infection, about 1 in 10,000. Almost all positives come from the uninfected
majority: the first term of $P(+)$ is $10^{-6}$ and the second is about
$10^{-2}$, so the second dominates. In counts, among 100 million people
the 100 infected all test positive, along with about a million
uninfected people.

Ignoring how rare the condition is (the prior probability) is called
the **base rate fallacy**. The test's accuracy, $P(+ \mid I) = 1$,
answers "if infected, will the test catch it?", not "if positive, am I
infected?".

The widget runs the same calculation for 10,000 samples. Think of a
test for a condition, such as an invasive species in a water sample:
prevalence is the fraction of samples that truly contain it.

```{r screening-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("screening.html")
```

> **Question:** Start at the default settings. Move sensitivity across
> its full range, then put it back and do the same with the false
> positive rate. Which one matters more for
> $P(\text{present} \mid +)$, and why? What happens when the false
> positive rate is 0?

## 4. More than two hypotheses {#many-hypotheses}

With hypotheses $H_1, H_2, \ldots$ that are mutually exclusive and
cover all possibilities, the law of total probability expands the
denominator into a sum (Bolker eq. 4.3.7):

$$P(H_i \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid H_i)\,P(H_i)}{\sum_j P(D \mid H_j)\,P(H_j)}.$$

The parts have names. $P(H_i)$ is the **prior**, $P(D \mid H_i)$ the
**likelihood**, $P(H_i \mid D)$ the **posterior**, and the denominator
makes the posteriors add to 1.

**Liana infestation** (Bolker 4.3.2). Saplings in a tropical forest
fall into four liana classes, from liana-free to heavily infested. In
the forest as a whole the classes make up 50%, 25%, 20%, and 5% of
saplings. A new sapling has 3 infested neighbors; field data say the
chance of 3 infested neighbors is 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.6 for saplings
in each class.

```{r liana}
prior <- c(0.50, 0.25, 0.20, 0.05)
lik <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.30, 0.60)       # P(3 infested neighbors | class)
post <- lik * prior / sum(lik * prior)
round(rbind(prior, likelihood = lik, posterior = post), 3)
sum(lik)                               # likelihoods need not add to 1
```

```{r liana-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
barplot(rbind(prior, post), beside = TRUE, col = c("grey75", "steelblue"),
        border = NA, names.arg = c("liana-free", "light", "moderate", "heavy"),
        xlab = "Liana class", ylab = "Probability", ylim = c(0, 0.55))
legend("topright", c("prior", "posterior, 3 infested neighbors"),
       fill = c("grey75", "steelblue"), border = NA, bty = "n")
```

The chance the sapling is heavily infested rises from 0.05 to
`r f2(post[4])`. The likelihoods add to `r sum(lik)`, not 1: each comes
from a different class, so they are not a probability distribution over
the classes. Multiplying by the prior and dividing by the total
converts them into one.

The prior here is a frequency, the share of each class in the forest,
so nobody disputes it. Disagreement between Bayesian and frequentist
statisticians starts when the hypotheses are values of a parameter
(a survival rate, a slope) and the prior expresses a degree of belief
rather than a frequency. That use of Bayes' rule is covered with
[Bayesian inference](Week7_IntervalsAndBayes.html#grid).

> **Question:** Suppose you knew nothing about how common each class
> is and gave all four the same prior, 0.25. What would the posterior
> for heavy infestation be? Why is it so different from
> `r f2(post[4])`?

## Discussion

1. In an [xkcd comic](https://xkcd.com/1132/), a detector reports
   whether the sun has gone nova. It rolls two dice and lies if both
   come up six (probability 1/36); otherwise it tells the truth. It
   says "yes." A frequentist notes that this answer has probability
   1/36 < 0.05 if the sun is fine, and concludes the sun has exploded.
   Write the problem as Bayes' rule. How large would the prior
   probability of a nova have to be for the posterior to pass 0.5?
2. In a nest-monitoring study, 80% of failed nests had a predator
   recorded on camera. A manager concludes that a nest with a predator
   on camera has an 80% chance of failing. Which conditional
   probability did the study measure, which one does the manager want,
   and what else would you need to know to get it?
3. A water sample from a reservoir where invasive mussels have never
   been found tests positive for their DNA. A second sample, taken the
   same day, also tests positive. How much should the second positive
   change your belief, and what could make the two results less
   independent than they look?

## Bonus: the Monty Hall problem {#monty-hall}

A game show has three doors, a car behind one and goats behind the
other two. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens
door 2 to show a goat, then offers you the chance to switch to door 3.
Should you?

Use Bayes' rule with three hypotheses (car behind door 1, 2, or 3),
each with prior 1/3. The data are "the host opened door 2." If the car
is behind door 1, the host could open door 2 or door 3, so the
likelihood is 1/2. If the car is behind door 2, he would never open it:
likelihood 0. If the car is behind door 3, door 2 is his only choice:
likelihood 1.

```{r monty-bayes}
prior_door <- rep(1/3, 3)
lik_door <- c(1/2, 0, 1)       # P(host opens door 2 | car behind door i)
lik_door * prior_door / sum(lik_door * prior_door)
```

Staying wins with probability 1/3 and switching with 2/3. A simulation
gives the same answer:

```{r monty-sim}
# one game; returns TRUE if the final choice has the car
play_monty <- function(switch_door) {
  doors <- 1:3
  car <- sample(doors, 1)
  pick <- sample(doors, 1)
  goats <- setdiff(doors, c(pick, car))          # doors the host may open
  opened <- goats[sample(length(goats), 1)]
  if (switch_door) pick <- setdiff(doors, c(pick, opened))
  pick == car
}

set.seed(31)
mean(replicate(10000, play_monty(switch_door = FALSE)))
mean(replicate(10000, play_monty(switch_door = TRUE)))
```

The widget plays the game with more doors. The host opens every door
except your pick and one other, never revealing the car.

```{r monty-widget, echo=FALSE}
widget("monty_hall.html")
```

## Bonus: many zeros from two processes {#zero-inflation}

Bolker (4.2) applies these rules to seed-removal stations. A predator
visits a station with probability $v$; if it visits, it takes each of
the $N$ seeds independently with probability $p$. Zero seeds can go
missing in two mutually exclusive ways: no visit, or a visit that takes
nothing. Adding them (law of total probability) gives

$$P(0 \text{ taken}) = (1 - v) + v\,(1 - p)^N, \qquad
P(x \text{ taken}) = v \binom{N}{x} p^x (1 - p)^{N - x} \;\; (x > 0).$$

```{r zero-inflated}
v <- 0.7
p_take <- 0.4
n_seeds <- 5
x_taken <- 0:n_seeds
p_zi <- v * dbinom(x_taken, n_seeds, p_take)
p_zi[1] <- p_zi[1] + (1 - v)
round(p_zi, 3)
sum(p_zi)
```

```{r zero-inflated-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
barplot(rbind(dbinom(x_taken, n_seeds, p_take), p_zi), beside = TRUE,
        names.arg = x_taken, col = c("grey75", "steelblue"), border = NA,
        xlab = "Seeds taken (of 5)", ylab = "Probability", ylim = c(0, 0.4))
legend("topright", c("binomial (predator always visits)", "zero-inflated (visits 70% of the time)"),
       fill = c("grey75", "steelblue"), border = NA, bty = "n")
```

The extra `r f2(1 - v)` of probability on zero comes from the stations
no predator found. Data with more zeros than a standard distribution
allows often have two processes behind them like this: one deciding
whether anything can happen, and one deciding how much.
